document.title: A Note on the Minimality of One-Way Functions in Post-Quantum Cryptography
document.venue_or_archive: IACR Communications in Cryptology, Vol. 1, No. 4 (received 2024-10-09, accepted 2024-12-03); also IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive, Report 2024/2095

candidate.title: Post-Quantum Minimality of One-Way Functions Under Non-Black-Box Security Reductions
candidate.subtitle: the classical implication is proved without a black-box reduction between the security games
candidate.one_line: If a cryptographic primitive classically implies one-way functions by any argument at all, rather than by a black-box reduction between the two security games, does the post-quantum-secure version of that primitive still imply post-quantum one-way functions?
candidate.informal: In classical cryptography, one-way functions are the minimal assumption: almost every basic primitive implies them. Post-quantum cryptography keeps the protocols classical but lets the attacker be quantum, and it is not obvious that the classical implications survive, because a classical proof that a primitive implies one-way functions typically works by taking an attacker on the one-way function and running it, repeatedly and from rewound states, to attack the primitive. Rewinding a quantum attacker is not generally possible. This paper shows the implications do survive whenever the classical proof is a black-box reduction between the two security games and the target primitive's security is defined by a two-message challenge-response game, which is the case for one-way functions; the argument replaces the quantum attacker by an equivalent stateful one that answers repeated questions consistently, so that rewinding it gains the reduction nothing and it becomes indistinguishable from an inefficient classical attacker the reduction was designed for. What the paper does not settle is the case where the classical implication is not proved by such a black-box reduction: the reduction may inspect the code of the attacker, and a quantum attacker has no classical code to inspect. The question is whether the classical implication still lifts, so that one-way functions are minimal for post-quantum cryptography with no restriction on how the classical proof was carried out.
candidate.formal_statement_latex:
Fix a class of efficient quantum adversaries $\mathsf{E} \in \{\mathrm{QPT}, \mathrm{QPT}/\mathrm{poly}\}$, and keep it fixed throughout.

Let $\mathcal{Q} = (F_{\mathcal{Q}}, R_{\mathcal{Q}})$ be any classical primitive with a game-based security definition (Definition~1), with challenger $C_{\mathcal{Q},f}$ and success threshold $t_{\mathcal{Q}}$, and let $\mathcal{F}$ be the one-way function primitive (Definition~3).

Suppose that a potentially non-constructive reduction from $\mathcal{F}$ to $\mathcal{Q}$ exists in the sense of Definition~4; equivalently, the classical existence of $\mathcal{Q}$ implies the classical existence of one-way functions. No assumption is made about how the security clause of Definition~4 is established: in particular, the passage from a $\mathrm{PPT}$ adversary $A_{\mathcal{F}}$ breaking $g_f$ to a $\mathrm{PPT}$ adversary $A_{\mathcal{Q}}$ breaking $f$ need \emph{not} be witnessed by a black-box reduction from winning in $C_{\mathcal{Q},f}$ to winning in $C_{\mathcal{F},g_f}$, and may depend arbitrarily on the code of $A_{\mathcal{F}}$.

Then: if the post-quantum variant $\mathcal{Q}'$ of $\mathcal{Q}$ against $\mathsf{E}$ exists (Definition~2), one-way functions secure against $\mathsf{E}$ exist, i.e.\ the post-quantum variant $\mathcal{F}'$ of $\mathcal{F}$ against $\mathsf{E}$ exists.
candidate.definitions_latex:
\begin{definition}[Game-based classical primitive]
A \emph{classical primitive} is a pair $\mathcal{P} = (F_{\mathcal{P}}, R_{\mathcal{P}})$, where $F_{\mathcal{P}}$ is a set of (possibly inefficient) randomized algorithms, called the correct implementations of $\mathcal{P}$, and $R_{\mathcal{P}}$ is a relation on pairs $(f, A)$ of algorithms; $(f,A) \in R_{\mathcal{P}}$ is read "$A$ $\mathcal{P}$-breaks $f$".

The primitive is \emph{game-based} if $R_{\mathcal{P}}$ is given by a security game: an interactive protocol, over classical communication, between a challenger $C_{\mathcal{P},f}$ (which may depend on the implementation $f$) and an adversary $A$, on common input the security parameter $1^n$, at the end of which $C_{\mathcal{P},f}$ outputs $1$ ("$A$ wins") or $0$; together with a \emph{success threshold} $t_{\mathcal{P}} : \mathbb{N} \to [0,1]$. Then $(f,A) \in R_{\mathcal{P}}$ iff there is a polynomial $p$ such that
$$\Pr[\,C_{\mathcal{P},f}(1^n) \text{ outputs } 1 \text{ against } A\,] \;\ge\; t_{\mathcal{P}}(n) + \tfrac{1}{p(n)}$$
for infinitely many $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Classical and post-quantum existence]
Let $\mathcal{P} = (F_{\mathcal{P}}, R_{\mathcal{P}})$ be a game-based classical primitive.

$\mathcal{P}$ \emph{exists classically} if there is a $\mathrm{PPT}$ implementation $f \in F_{\mathcal{P}}$ such that no $\mathrm{PPT}$ algorithm $A$ satisfies $(f,A) \in R_{\mathcal{P}}$.

The \emph{post-quantum variant} $\mathcal{P}'$ of $\mathcal{P}$ against a class $\mathsf{E}$ of efficient quantum adversaries is the same primitive with the same implementations and the same challenger $C_{\mathcal{P},f}$, with the adversary now ranging over $\mathsf{E}$; the communication with the challenger remains classical. Thus $\mathcal{P}'$ \emph{exists} if there is a $\mathrm{PPT}$ implementation $f \in F_{\mathcal{P}}$ such that no $A \in \mathsf{E}$ wins $C_{\mathcal{P},f}(1^n)$ with probability at least $t_{\mathcal{P}}(n) + 1/p(n)$ for any polynomial $p$ and infinitely many $n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[One-way functions as a game-based primitive]
The primitive $\mathcal{F} = (F_{\mathcal{F}}, R_{\mathcal{F}})$ of one-way functions has $F_{\mathcal{F}}$ equal to the set of all functions $f : \{0,1\}^* \to \{0,1\}^*$, viewed as deterministic algorithms; a $\mathrm{PPT}$ implementation is one computable in deterministic polynomial time.

Its security game is the $2$-message game with threshold $t_{\mathcal{F}} = 0$: on security parameter $1^n$ the challenger samples $x \leftarrow \{0,1\}^n$ and sends $f(x)$; the adversary replies with a single message $x'$; the challenger outputs $1$ iff $f(x') = f(x)$.

Hence $\mathcal{F}$ exists classically iff classical one-way functions exist, and $\mathcal{F}'$ exists against $\mathsf{E}$ iff there is a deterministic polynomial-time computable $f$ with $\Pr_{x \leftarrow \{0,1\}^n,\, x' \leftarrow A(f(x),1^n)}[f(x') = f(x)]$ negligible in $n$ for every $A \in \mathsf{E}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Potentially non-constructive reduction]
A \emph{potentially non-constructive reduction} from a classical primitive $\mathcal{P} = (F_{\mathcal{P}}, R_{\mathcal{P}})$ to a classical primitive $\mathcal{Q} = (F_{\mathcal{Q}}, R_{\mathcal{Q}})$ exists if both of the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Implementation.} For every $\mathrm{PPT}$ implementation $f \in F_{\mathcal{Q}}$ there is a $\mathrm{PPT}$ implementation $g_f \in F_{\mathcal{P}}$.
\item \emph{Security.} For every $\mathrm{PPT}$ implementation $f \in F_{\mathcal{Q}}$: if there is a $\mathrm{PPT}$ adversary $A_{\mathcal{P}}$ that $\mathcal{P}$-breaks $g_f$, then there is a $\mathrm{PPT}$ adversary $A_{\mathcal{Q}}$ that $\mathcal{Q}$-breaks $f$.
\end{enumerate}
Neither clause carries any black-box requirement; clause 2 is a bare existential statement, and is exactly the assertion that the classical existence of $\mathcal{Q}$ implies the classical existence of $\mathcal{P}$.

A reduction is additionally \emph{game-based black-box} if $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ are game-based and the existence of $A_{\mathcal{Q}}$ in clause 2 is established by a black-box reduction: a $\mathrm{PPT}$ oracle algorithm $\mathcal{R}$ such that for every (possibly inefficient) adversary $A$ winning in $C_{\mathcal{P},g_f}$ with non-negligible advantage above $t_{\mathcal{P}}$, the algorithm $\mathcal{R}^{A}$ wins in $C_{\mathcal{Q},f}$ with non-negligible advantage above $t_{\mathcal{Q}}$, where $\mathcal{R}$ may query $A$ on inputs of its choice, on several security parameters, and may rewind $A$ or reset its randomness.
\end{definition}
candidate.notation_latex:
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ is the security parameter. A function is \emph{negligible} if it is eventually smaller than $1/p(n)$ for every polynomial $p$; a probability is \emph{non-negligible} otherwise.

$\mathrm{PPT}$ denotes a classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm.

$\mathrm{QPT}$ denotes a uniform efficient quantum algorithm with classical inputs and outputs: a family $\{Q_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of quantum circuits of size $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ whose descriptions are produced by a $\mathrm{PPT}$ machine on input $1^n$, with work registers initialized to $|0\rangle$ and the output register measured in the computational basis.

$\mathrm{QPT}/\mathrm{poly}$ denotes the non-uniform variant: the same, except the work registers of $Q_n$ are initialized with a quantum advice state $|\phi_n\rangle$ on $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ qubits, depending only on $n$.

$\mathsf{E}$ ranges over $\{\mathrm{QPT}, \mathrm{QPT}/\mathrm{poly}\}$ and denotes the class of efficient quantum adversaries fixed in the statement.

$\mathcal{P} = (F_{\mathcal{P}}, R_{\mathcal{P}})$ denotes a classical primitive, with $F_{\mathcal{P}}$ its set of correct implementations and $R_{\mathcal{P}}$ its breaking relation; $C_{\mathcal{P},f}$ is its challenger on implementation $f$ and $t_{\mathcal{P}}$ its success threshold. $\mathcal{P}'$ denotes the post-quantum variant of $\mathcal{P}$.

$\mathcal{Q}$ and $\mathcal{Q}'$ denote the primitive in the hypothesis and its post-quantum variant; $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{F}'$ denote the one-way function primitive and its post-quantum variant.

$f$ denotes an implementation of $\mathcal{Q}$ and $g_f$ the implementation of $\mathcal{F}$ obtained from it; $A$, $A_{\mathcal{P}}$, $A_{\mathcal{Q}}$, $A_{\mathcal{F}}$ denote adversaries, and $\mathcal{R}$ a black-box reduction.

parameters.meaning: Security parameter; all efficiency and negligibility are asymptotic in it.

The fixed class of efficient quantum adversaries, either uniform ($\mathrm{QPT}$) or non-uniform with polynomial-size quantum advice ($\mathrm{QPT}/\mathrm{poly}$). The conjecture is asserted for each choice separately.
An arbitrary classical primitive with a game-based security definition, quantified universally.
The success threshold of $\mathcal{Q}$'s security game; unrestricted (it may be $0$, $1/2$, or anything else).
A $\mathrm{PPT}$ implementation of $\mathcal{Q}$, and the $\mathrm{PPT}$ implementation of one-way functions built from it by the implementation clause of the reduction.

candidate.setting_latex:
One-way functions are the minimal assumption of classical cryptography: Impagliazzo and Luby showed that identification protocols, symmetric-key encryption, commitments and coin flipping all imply them \cite{IL89}, and the standard way such implications are established is a black-box reduction, which uses the primitive and the adversary as oracles and therefore relativizes \cite{RTV04}. Non-black-box security reductions, which exploit the code of the adversary, exist but are comparatively rare \cite{Bar01}.

Quantum cryptography appears to have a different assumption hierarchy: there are oracles relative to which pseudorandom quantum states exist while $\mathbf{BQP} = \mathbf{QMA}$ \cite{Kre21}, and a classical oracle relative to which single-copy pseudorandom states exist while $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{NP}$ \cite{KQST23}, so quantum analogues of one-way functions may not sit at the base. \emph{Post-quantum} cryptography is the intermediate regime: protocols and challengers stay classical, but adversaries are quantum. Whether the classical hierarchy survives there is not automatic, because a classical security reduction may rewind its adversary, and rewinding destroys the internal state of a quantum one. This is the difficulty that work on constructive post-quantum reductions \cite{BBK22} and on universal reductions relative to stateful oracles \cite{CFP22} addresses, in both cases under restrictions on the reduction (single-copy adversaries, non-adaptivity, or straight-line behaviour).

The present paper removes those restrictions on the \emph{reduction} and instead restricts the \emph{game}. Its main theorem: if a classical black-box game-based security reduction proves that $\mathcal{Q}$ implies a primitive $\mathcal{P}$ whose security game has only two messages, then any efficient quantum adversary breaking $\mathcal{P}$ can be turned into an efficient quantum adversary breaking $\mathcal{Q}$, so the implication lifts. The technique replaces the quantum adversary by a lazily-evaluated, memoizing version, which answers repeated queries identically and is therefore statistically indistinguishable, even under rewinding and resetting, from an inefficient classical adversary of the same advantage; a two-message game asks the adversary only one question, so this modification costs nothing in advantage. Since one-way functions have a two-message falsifiable game, every primitive that classically implies one-way functions by a black-box game-based reduction implies post-quantum one-way functions post-quantumly, for uniform and non-uniform quantum adversaries alike, and even when the reduction assumes its adversary is deterministic.

The hypothesis that the security reduction is black-box is what makes the whole argument possible: the proof works by substituting a doctored adversary into $\mathcal{R}$ as an oracle. When the classical implication from $\mathcal{Q}$ to one-way functions is proved some other way, the paper's machinery has nothing to substitute into, and the paper records this case as unresolved. Note that the paper's results are already insensitive to how the \emph{implementation} is built from $\mathcal{Q}$: that may be arbitrarily non-black-box. Only the security direction is constrained.
candidate.status_note: Settled affirmatively whenever the classical implication from $\mathcal{Q}$ to one-way functions is witnessed by a black-box reduction between the two security games, with the implementation reduction arbitrary, for both uniform and non-uniform quantum adversaries and also for reductions that assume a deterministic adversary. Open when that security implication is not witnessed by such a black-box reduction; the paper takes no position on which way it goes.
candidate.progress_note: Theorem 1 lifts any classical black-box reduction from a game $\mathcal{Q}$ to a $2$-message game $\mathcal{P}$ to the post-quantum setting, uniformly and non-uniformly. Theorem 3 turns this into a statement about primitives, and Corollary 1 specialises it to $\mathcal{P} = $ one-way functions, with no restriction on how the reduction calls its adversary, because the one-way function game is falsifiable. Theorem 2 extends the lifting to reductions that assume their oracle adversary is deterministic, under any one of three side conditions ($\mathcal{Q}$ threshold-zero with single-security-parameter calls; $\mathcal{P}$ falsifiable; $\mathcal{Q}$ falsifiable with single-security-parameter calls). In the other direction, the paper observes that the $2$-message restriction on $\mathcal{P}$ cannot simply be dropped: a contrived primitive built from the $4$-message qubit certification test of Brakerski et al.\ is implied by LWE classically through a black-box reduction but, the paper argues, not post-quantumly unless LWE is quantumly broken.

quotes.text: Our work leaves open answering our main question when Q implies OWFs through a non-black-box security reduction, or when P uses a more complicated security game than a two-message one.
If a classically secure cryptographic primitive Q implies one-way functions, does the post-quantum-secure variant of P imply (post-quantum) one-way functions as well?

Then, we define the post-quantum variant of P to be the same primitive, but now the security definition allows efficient quantum adversaries to participate in the same security game (using classical communication).

This means that our results do not depend on how the implementation reduction is performed, as formalized in [RTV04], meaning that we can handle non-black-box constructions, so long as the security reduction is a black-box reduction between games.

Finally, with this definition in hand, we can conclude that if the existence of some cryptographic primitive implies the existence of one-way functions classically through a black-box reduction between their security games, then the implication also holds in the post-quantum setting.
To derive Corollary 1 from Theorem 3 we merely observe that one-way functions have a 2-message security game and that their security game is falsifiable.
In fact, non-black-box security reductions à la [Bar01] are less common in cryptography.

candidate.why_interesting: This is the paper's headline question — "Are one-way functions minimal for post-quantum cryptography?" — with the one caveat the paper needed removed. As things stand, post-quantum minimality of one-way functions is a theorem about a class of proofs, not about the primitives: it holds for every implication that happens to have been established by a black-box reduction between games. A positive answer would make the statement unconditional in the way the classical one is, putting post-quantum one-way functions at the base of the post-quantum hierarchy for every primitive that classically implies them, regardless of how that classical implication was proved. A negative answer would be at least as informative, and the paper hands over a template for how one would look: exhibit a primitive that plausibly exists post-quantumly while post-quantum one-way functions do not, with the classical implication going through non-black-box, which would mean the classical assumption hierarchy genuinely does not survive contact with quantum adversaries even when the protocols stay classical.
candidate.why_clean: The statement is exactly Corollary 1 of the paper with a single hypothesis deleted, and both halves — the hypothesis (a classical implication in the sense of the paper's Definition 8) and the conclusion (existence of post-quantum one-way functions) — are standard notions definable from scratch in half a page. There is no auxiliary construction, no parameter to tune, and no unpublished machinery: the paper's own definitions are all a reader needs, and the theorem proved next to it shows precisely which hypothesis is doing the work.
candidate.risks: The main thing a reviewer should press on is whether this is a problem or a programme. The paper poses it as a question but gives no account of what makes the non-black-box case hard, and offers no partial result towards it. "Non-black-box security reduction" is not a structured class the way black-box reductions are; the hypothesis of the conjecture, as the paper's Definition 8 makes explicit, is just the bare implication "$\mathcal{Q}$ classically exists $\Rightarrow$ one-way functions classically exist", so a positive proof would have to be a general lifting theorem with no reduction structure to grip. The honest reading may be that the affirmative direction is not attackable, and only the refuting direction (a contrived primitive, in the style of the paper's own $4$-message counterexample) has a visible line of attack. A second point: the paper leaves it open without conjecturing a direction, so phrasing it affirmatively is a site convention, not the authors' claim, and a solver should treat both directions as live. Third, I have not checked the literature after December 2024 for a resolution, and the paper is short and recent enough that a follow-up could exist. Finally, the third "Furthermore" clause of Corollary 1 (deterministic-adversary reductions) is asserted for one-way functions on the strength of the falsifiability of the one-way function game; I have kept the conjecture free of any deterministic-adversary hypothesis, matching the black-box statement the paper proves.

grounding.quote: Our work leaves open answering our main question when Q implies OWFs through a non-black-box security reduction, or when P uses a more complicated security game than a two-message one.
If a classically secure cryptographic primitive Q implies one-way functions, does the post-quantum-secure variant of P imply (post-quantum) one-way functions as well?

Then, we define the post-quantum variant of P to be the same primitive, but now the security definition allows efficient quantum adversaries to participate in the same security game (using classical communication).

This means that our results do not depend on how the implementation reduction is performed, as formalized in [RTV04], meaning that we can handle non-black-box constructions, so long as the security reduction is a black-box reduction between games.

Finally, with this definition in hand, we can conclude that if the existence of some cryptographic primitive implies the existence of one-way functions classically through a black-box reduction between their security games, then the implication also holds in the post-quantum setting.
To derive Corollary 1 from Theorem 3 we merely observe that one-way functions have a 2-message security game and that their security game is falsifiable.
In fact, non-black-box security reductions à la [Bar01] are less common in cryptography.

checks.name: existence
checks.finding: The problem is the paper's own, stated in the abstract: "Our work leaves open answering our main question when Q implies OWFs through a non-black-box security reduction, or when P uses a more complicated security game than a two-message one." The framing question is restated on p.3 ("If a classically secure cryptographic primitive Q implies one-way functions, does the post-quantum-secure variant of P imply (post-quantum) one-way functions as well?" -- the paper's own P/Q slip, which the draft quotes verbatim rather than silently fixing).

checks.name: openness
checks.finding: It stays open through the whole paper. Corollary 1 (p.22), the paper's terminal statement about OWFs, carries "through a black-box game-based reduction" inside its hypothesis; Theorem 3 (p.21) likewise requires "the security reduction is black-box between their games"; Theorem 1 (p.15) and Theorem 2 (p.17) both start from a classical reduction R used as an oracle machine. Section 4 ends on p.22, references run p.23-26, and there is no appendix, so nothing later resolves it. The only other open item the paper flags (P with more than 2 messages, p.1 and p.7) is a different branch that the draft does not stake its statement on.

checks.name: strength
checks.finding: The formal statement is Corollary 1 (p.22) with exactly the black-box hypothesis deleted: same hypothesis (Q game-based, classical existence of Q implies classical existence of OWFs, implementation arbitrary), same conclusion (post-quantum variant of Q exists implies post-quantum OWFs exist), same uniform/non-uniform pairing. It is stated for all classical implications rather than only non-black-box ones, so it nominally includes the already-proved black-box case; since that case is settled by Corollary 1, this is not a strengthening in substance, and the subtitle and status_note make the residue explicit. Restricting Q to game-based primitives is not a weakening either: Definition 7 (p.11) only defines a post-quantum variant for game-based primitives, so the statement would not typecheck otherwise.

checks.name: quantifiers-and-parameters
checks.finding: Checked symbol by symbol. The "resp." pairing of Theorem 3 and Corollary 1 (p.21-22) is rendered correctly as a single class E fixed throughout, not as a mixed uniform-hypothesis/non-uniform-conclusion claim. Definition 4 reproduces Definition 8's clause order and per-implementation quantification ("For every PPT implementation f in F_Q there is a PPT implementation g_f in F_P"; "For every PPT f: if there is a PPT A_P that P-breaks g_f, then there is a PPT A_Q that Q-breaks f", p.11). The reduction direction is right: an adversary against C_{F,g_f} feeds R, R wins C_{Q,f} (p.10 Def 5 convention, p.12 bullet). "Non-negligible advantage above threshold" is unpacked correctly as "exists p, infinitely many n" (p.8, p.9, p.11). Non-uniform QPT/poly keeps PPT-generated circuit descriptions and changes only the initial work-register state, matching p.9; the paper's "polynomially more quantum advice" cost (p.4) stays inside the class.

checks.name: attribution
checks.finding: This is Buxbaum-Mahmoody's own open question ("Our work leaves open answering our main question", p.1), not a problem inherited from a cited work. Prior work is correctly kept as prior work in setting_latex: IL89 (p.2), RTV04 (p.2), Bar01 (p.2), BBK22/CFP22 (p.6-7), Kre21/KQST23 (p.2). All seven bibliography entries match what is printed on p.23-26 as claimed.

checks.name: definitions
checks.finding: Two defects. (a) The "game-based black-box" clause of the draft's Definition 4 omits that R is given 1^{1/eps} as an input parameter (Def 5, p.10, and footnote 8: without it "the reduction might not even get one 'useful' execution out of its adversary"), and softens the paper's condition that the oracle adversary wins in G_1 with advantage eps(n_1) "for all security parameters n_1" to "non-negligible advantage". The omitted input is load-bearing in the paper's own proof: p.18 says "it will be crucial here that we know eps (given to R as input) as stated in Definitions 5 and 9". As written the draft's status_note therefore claims a settled region wider than the paper establishes. (b) The closing remark of Definition 4 says clause 2 "is exactly the assertion that the classical existence of Q implies the classical existence of P", and the formal statement says "equivalently"; this presents a one-directional implication as an equivalence (see p.11, where the paper says only that the definition "formalizes what it means for a primitive's existence to imply that of another"). Everything else checks: game-based primitive (Def 4/6/7, p.9-11), falsifiable = polynomial-time challenger (p.9), threshold-zero OWF game (p.9, p.22), OWF definition (Def 10, p.22).

checks.name: fabrication
checks.finding: The informal asserts, as the reason the non-black-box case resists, that "a quantum attacker has no classical code to inspect". Definition 2 (p.8) defines an efficient quantum algorithm as a circuit family {Q_n} "where the description of Q_n is computed by a classical PPT algorithm A given input 1^n" -- so a QPT adversary does have classical code; only the non-uniform advice state |phi_n> (p.9) lacks a classical description. The paper never offers any diagnosis of why the non-black-box case is open. Relatedly, "the paper's machinery has nothing to substitute into, and the paper records this case as unresolved" (setting_latex) mixes the draft's own inference with the paper's record. Everything else asserted checks out: Theorem 1 (p.15), Theorem 2 with its three cases (p.17), Theorem 3 (p.21), Corollary 1 including "even if the reduction assumes its adversaries to be deterministic" (p.22), the lazy-evaluation/memoization technique (Algorithm 2 and Lemma 3, p.14-15), and the contrived 4-message BCM+21-based counterexample implied by LWE classically but not post-quantumly unless LWE breaks (p.7).

checks.name: self-containment
checks.finding: The statement is provable from what is given: all four internal definitions are supplied, and the notation block defines n, negligible, PPT, QPT, QPT/poly, E, and every symbol used (Q, Q', F, F', f, g_f, C_{P,f}, t_P, R). The internal Definition numbering does not match the paper's (the paper's Definitions 1, 3, 4 are Classical Algorithms, Classical Interface, Security Games), but it is internally consistent, so a reader who has never seen the paper knows what to prove.

corrections.problem: The clause omits that the reduction is given 1^{1/eps} as an input parameter, and states the oracle adversary's success as "non-negligible advantage" instead of the paper's "advantage eps(n_1) for all security parameters n_1" (Def 5, p.10, with footnote 8 explaining the input is needed for non-vacuity, and p.18 stating that knowing eps is crucial to the proof of Theorem 2, Case 2). The looser clause makes the black-box case, and hence the region the status_note reports as settled, wider than the paper proves.
corrections.corrected: ... the existence of A_Q in clause 2 is established by a black-box reduction: a PPT oracle algorithm R that is additionally given 1^{1/eps} as an input parameter, such that for every (possibly inefficient) adversary A winning in C_{P,g_f} with advantage eps(n_1) >= 1/poly(n_1) at every security parameter n_1, the algorithm R^A wins in C_{Q,f} with advantage delta_eps >= 1/poly(n_2) above t_Q, where R may query A on inputs of its choice, on several security parameters, and may rewind A or reset its randomness.

corrections.problem: "equivalently, the classical existence of Q implies the classical existence of one-way functions" and "clause 2 is a bare existential statement, and is exactly the assertion that the classical existence of Q implies the classical existence of P" state an equivalence where only one direction holds. Definition 8 (p.11) is a per-implementation condition quantified over every PPT f in F_Q; it yields existence-implies-existence, but existence-implies-existence does not yield a map f -> g_f with the security property. The paper claims only that the definition "formalizes what it means for a primitive's existence to imply that of another" (p.11).
corrections.corrected: In the formal statement: "...exists in the sense of Definition 4; this is the paper's formalization of the classical existence of Q implying the classical existence of one-way functions, and in particular it entails that implication." In Definition 4: "Neither clause carries any black-box requirement; clause 2 is a bare existential statement, and clauses 1 and 2 together entail that the classical existence of Q implies the classical existence of P."

corrections.problem: "the reduction may inspect the code of the attacker, and a quantum attacker has no classical code to inspect" is contradicted by the paper's own Definition 2 (p.8), where an efficient quantum algorithm is a circuit family whose descriptions are computed by a classical PPT algorithm; and the paper offers no diagnosis of why the non-black-box case is open.
corrections.corrected: Delete the claim, or restrict it: "...the reduction may inspect the code of the attacker, and while a uniform quantum attacker is still generated by classical code, its state -- and, in the non-uniform case, its quantum advice -- has no classical description. The paper does not say why this case resists; it simply records it as unresolved."

fabrications: "a quantum attacker has no classical code to inspect" (informal) -- contradicted by Definition 2, p.8, where an efficient quantum algorithm is a circuit family whose descriptions are computed by a classical PPT algorithm on input 1^n; only the non-uniform advice state |phi_n> (p.9) lacks a classical description.

"the paper's machinery has nothing to substitute into" and the implication that the paper explains why the non-black-box case is open (setting_latex) -- the paper records the case as open (p.1) but offers no reason anywhere; this is the draft's own inference presented as the paper's.
verify.reason: The problem is genuinely the paper's and genuinely survives to the end: the abstract on p.1 records it as left open, and every result that could close it (Theorem 1 p.15, Theorem 2 p.17, Theorem 3 p.21, Corollary 1 p.22) carries the black-box hypothesis inside its statement, with no appendix after the p.23-26 references. The formal statement is Corollary 1 with exactly that hypothesis removed, and the quantifiers most likely to be corrupted -- the uniform/non-uniform "resp." pairing and Definition 8's per-implementation clauses -- are correct. The single most important defect is in the draft's own definition of a game-based black-box reduction: it drops the 1^{1/eps} input that Definition 5 and footnote 8 (p.10) require and that p.18 calls crucial to the proof, which inflates the region the draft reports as already settled; that plus the "equivalently" overstatement of Definition 8 and the fabricated "no classical code to inspect" gloss are all precisely repairable.
